entries.title: Monarchy
entries.summary: Rule by a single hereditary sovereign.
entries.description: A monarchy vests supreme authority in a single ruler who inherits the throne through bloodline. Variants include absolute monarchy (unchecked power), constitutional monarchy (limited by law), and elective monarchy (ruler chosen by a council). Power transitions through birth, marriage, or conquest.
examples: Fantasy: Gondor in Lord of the Rings
entries.writing_tips: Succession crises, the tension between duty and desire, and courtiers jockeying for influence. Monarchies create natural stakes around heirs, marriage alliances, and usurpers.

entries.title: Feudalism
entries.summary: Decentralized system where lords grant land in exchange for loyalty and military service.
entries.description: Land (fiefs) flows downward from a monarch through vassals to serfs. Each lord governs their territory with significant autonomy, owing fealty and military support upward. This creates layered loyalties and frequent power struggles between nominal allies.
examples: Fantasy: A Song of Ice and Fire
entries.writing_tips: Vassals may be more powerful than their nominal liege, oaths can conflict, and peasant revolts simmer beneath the surface. Great for political intrigue plots.

entries.title: Theocracy
entries.summary: Government led by religious authority claiming divine mandate.
entries.description: Political power derives from religious doctrine. The head of state is a religious leader or claims to rule on behalf of a deity. Laws are derived from sacred texts. Dissent can be framed as heresy. The church and state are inseparable.
examples: Fantasy: The Magisterium in His Dark Materials
entries.writing_tips: Tension between faith and free thought. Characters who question doctrine face existential stakes. The gap between clergy ideals and political reality drives conflict.

entries.title: Republic
entries.summary: Power held by elected representatives acting on behalf of citizens.
entries.description: Citizens elect representatives to govern. Can range from democratic republics with broad suffrage to oligarchic republics where only elites vote. Separation of powers, term limits, and constitutions define the structure.
examples: Fantasy: The Republic in Star Wars
entries.writing_tips: Political maneuvering, factionalism, and the corruption of ideals. Election fraud, populist demagogues, and legislative gridlock are rich story material.

entries.title: Tribal Council
entries.summary: Governance through consensus among tribal elders or chiefs.
entries.description: Authority rests with a council of elders, clan heads, or a chief advised by respected members. Decisions are often made through deliberation and consensus rather than decree. Oral tradition and custom carry the weight of law.
examples: Fantasy: Dothraki in A Song of Ice and Fire
entries.writing_tips: Personal relationships, honor debts, and oral history. Internal politics revolve around respect, prowess, and lineage rather than wealth or bureaucracy.

entries.title: Magocracy
entries.summary: Rule by magic users, where political power derives from arcane ability.
entries.description: Only those with magical talent can hold office or citizenship. Society stratifies by magical aptitude. Non-magic users may be second-class citizens. The ruling body may be a council of archmages or a sorcerer-king.
examples: Fantasy: Tevinter Imperium in Dragon Age
entries.writing_tips: Questions about innate vs. earned power, discrimination against the magically inert, and what happens when magic fades or is disrupted.

entries.title: Oligarchy
entries.summary: Rule by a small group of powerful individuals — wealthy families, military leaders, or merchant princes.
entries.description: A handful of families or organizations control the state. Power passes within these elite circles. May appear democratic but elections are controlled. Wealth, connections, and blackmail maintain the status quo.
entries.writing_tips: Rival oligarchs make excellent antagonists. Characters born into the system who question it, or outsiders trying to break in, create compelling arcs.

entries.title: Anarchy / Stateless Society
entries.summary: Absence of formal government; communities self-organize through mutual aid or might.
entries.description: No central authority. Order maintained through community agreement, personal reputation, or threat of violence. Can be utopian (cooperative communes) or dystopian (warlord territories). Often transitional after collapse of prior government.
entries.writing_tips: Anarchy forces characters to rely on themselves and small groups. Trust becomes the most valuable currency. The question of 'who protects the weak?' drives moral conflict.

entries.title: Military Junta
entries.summary: Government controlled by military officers who seized power through force.
entries.description: The military rules directly, often after a coup. A general or council of officers holds supreme power. Civil liberties are typically suspended. Dissent is met with force. The junta may promise elections that never come.
entries.writing_tips: Juntas create a world of surveillance, curfews, and resistance cells. The tension between soldiers who believe they're saving the country and those they oppress is potent.

entries.title: Caste System
entries.summary: Rigid social hierarchy where birth determines status and occupation.
entries.description: Society is divided into hereditary groups with specific roles and privileges. Movement between castes is forbidden or extremely rare. Each caste has defined occupations, marriage restrictions, and social interactions.
entries.writing_tips: Characters who don't fit, forbidden relationships across castes, and revolutionaries who challenge the order create immediate tension.

entries.title: Guild System
entries.summary: Organized trade associations controlling crafts, commerce, and professional standards.
entries.description: Guilds regulate apprenticeship, set prices, maintain quality, and wield political influence. Master craftsmen hold authority. Guilds may control entire economic sectors and serve as de facto local government.
entries.writing_tips: Guilds provide natural factions with their own politics, rivalries, and secrets. A thieves' guild, assassins' guild, or merchants' guild each offer distinct story possibilities.

entries.title: Nomadic Society
entries.summary: People who move seasonally following resources, with portable culture and governance.
entries.description: No permanent settlements. Society organized around herds, trade routes, or seasonal resources. Possessions are portable. Status comes from skill, herds, or reputation. Oral tradition is paramount.
examples: Fantasy: Aiel in Wheel of Time
entries.writing_tips: Nomads clash with settled peoples over land and values. Their mobility makes them hard to conquer. Honor, hospitality laws, and oral history define their culture.

entries.title: Matriarchy / Patriarchy
entries.summary: Society structured around gender-based authority and inheritance lines.
entries.description: In a matriarchy, women hold primary power and property passes through the female line. In a patriarchy, men dominate. Both create specific expectations, restrictions, and rebellion opportunities for characters who don't conform.
entries.writing_tips: Subverting or questioning gender-based power structures is rich terrain. Characters who excel in roles 'not meant for them' face both internal and external conflict.

entries.title: Meritocracy
entries.summary: Status and power earned through demonstrated ability, achievement, or examination.
entries.description: Advancement based on talent and effort rather than birth. Imperial examination systems, competitive trials, or demonstrated skill determine rank. In theory egalitarian, but in practice often biased by access to education and resources.
entries.writing_tips: Meritocracies create pressure to perform and the temptation to cheat. The gap between meritocratic ideals and the reality of privilege makes for compelling social critique.

entries.title: Slave Society
entries.summary: Economy and social order dependent on enslaved labor.
entries.description: A significant portion of the population is legally owned as property. Slavery may be hereditary, based on conquest, debt, or birth. Slave revolts, underground networks, and abolitionist movements are inherent tensions.
examples: Fantasy: Slaver's Bay in A Song of Ice and Fire
entries.writing_tips: Handle with care and research. Focus on the humanity, agency, and resistance of enslaved characters rather than their suffering. Examine the moral corruption of slaveholders.

entries.title: Hard Magic
entries.summary: Magic with clearly defined rules, costs, and limitations that readers can understand and predict.
entries.description: The magic system operates like a science: specific inputs produce specific outputs. Users and readers understand what magic can and cannot do. Limitations are as important as abilities. Solving problems with magic feels earned because the reader understands the constraints.
entries.writing_tips: Hard magic needs consistent rules established BEFORE they solve plot problems (Sanderson's First Law). The limitations create the drama.

entries.title: Soft Magic
entries.summary: Magic that is mysterious, wondrous, and not fully explained to the reader.
entries.description: The rules of magic are deliberately vague or unknown. Magic inspires wonder and awe rather than strategic problem-solving. It should never conveniently solve problems without cost or buildup.
examples: Gandalf's magic in Lord of the Rings
entries.writing_tips: Soft magic should create problems more often than it solves them. Use it for atmosphere, wonder, and raising stakes.

entries.title: Blood Magic / Sacrifice Magic
entries.summary: Power drawn from life force, blood, or willing/unwilling sacrifice.
entries.description: Magic requires a tangible physical cost: blood, pain, life force, or the sacrifice of something precious. The greater the sacrifice, the greater the power. Creates inherent moral tension and escalating stakes.
entries.writing_tips: The moral cost is the story. Characters must decide how much they're willing to pay and who pays the price.

entries.title: Elemental Magic
entries.summary: Power over natural elements such as fire, water, earth, air, and their combinations.
entries.description: Practitioners control one or more natural elements. Affinity may be innate, cultural, or chosen. Elements can be classical (four), Eastern (five), or expanded to include light, shadow, metal, ice, etc.
entries.writing_tips: Elemental systems lend themselves to personality-element pairings and cultural divisions. Consider how elements interact and what happens at boundaries.

entries.title: Runic / Inscription Magic
entries.summary: Power channeled through written symbols, glyphs, or geometric patterns.
entries.description: Magic activated by writing, carving, or drawing specific symbols. The precision of the inscription matters. Mistakes can be catastrophic. Literacy and magical ability are linked. Ancient ruins may contain powerful forgotten runes.
examples: Name of the Wind sympathy bindings
entries.writing_tips: Runic magic rewards preparation over improvisation. A mage's workshop and library become important. Discovering forgotten runes drives exploration plots.

entries.title: Divine / Prayer Magic
entries.summary: Power granted by deities or higher beings in response to devotion or bargains.
entries.description: Magic comes from a divine source: a god, spirit, or cosmic entity. The practitioner serves as a conduit. Power may be granted, revoked, or come with divine mandates. Clerics, paladins, and warlocks fit this model.
entries.writing_tips: Divine magic creates a three-way relationship: character, deity, and world. What happens when a god's demands conflict with the character's conscience?

entries.title: Psychic / Mental Powers
entries.summary: Abilities originating from the mind — telepathy, telekinesis, precognition, and mind control.
entries.description: Power comes from mental discipline, genetic mutation, or evolutionary development rather than external sources. Often has physical costs like nosebleeds, exhaustion, or madness. Social implications of mind-reading are enormous.
entries.writing_tips: Psychic powers raise privacy and consent issues. Telepaths are feared and isolated. Precognition creates paradoxes. The social implications are often more interesting than the combat applications.

entries.title: Alchemy / Transmutation
entries.summary: Transforming substances through quasi-scientific magical processes.
entries.description: The precursor to chemistry combined with magical theory. Practitioners transform materials, create potions, and seek fundamental truths like the philosopher's stone. Requires reagents, equipment, and knowledge. Results are physical, tangible objects.
entries.writing_tips: Alchemy bridges magic and science. The quest for forbidden knowledge (turning lead to gold, achieving immortality) drives character obsession and moral compromise.

entries.title: Archipelago
entries.summary: A chain or cluster of islands, each potentially with distinct culture and ecology.
entries.description: Islands create natural isolation, breeding distinct cultures, languages, and species on each. Maritime trade and naval power become paramount. Control of sea lanes determines economic and military dominance.
entries.writing_tips: Each island can be a self-contained world. Sea voyages create natural journey structure. Island isolation breeds unique customs and secrets.

entries.title: Underground / Subterranean
entries.summary: Civilizations built in caves, tunnels, or beneath the earth's surface.
entries.description: Entire societies existing underground, whether by choice or necessity. Architecture carved from living rock. Bioluminescence, fungi forests, and underground rivers provide ecosystem. Darkness shapes culture and senses.
entries.writing_tips: Claustrophobia, light as precious resource, adapted senses, and the psychology of never seeing sky. Cave-ins are ever-present danger.

entries.title: Floating / Aerial
entries.summary: Landmasses, cities, or civilizations suspended in the sky.
entries.description: Whether through magic, technology, or natural phenomenon, terrain exists above the ground. Creates vertical society, fear of falling, and dependence on flight. Ground below may be dangerous, forbidden, or mythologized.
entries.writing_tips: Verticality creates natural class metaphors (higher = elite). Falling is the ultimate threat. Consider supplies, waste, and the relationship with ground-dwellers.

entries.title: Desert / Wasteland
entries.summary: Arid regions where water is life's most precious resource.
entries.description: Extreme heat, vast distances, and scarce resources define desert societies. Water rights drive politics. Navigation requires specialized knowledge. Oases become strategic strongpoints. Sandstorms are deadly events.
entries.writing_tips: Water scarcity creates immediate, constant stakes. Desert peoples develop water-conservation culture, stillsuits, and deep well knowledge. The desert strips everything to essentials.

entries.title: Tundra / Arctic
entries.summary: Frozen landscapes where cold is the constant enemy and survival demands adaptation.
entries.description: Permafrost, ice sheets, and extreme cold define life. Short growing seasons, long winters, and limited resources. Survival requires specialized clothing, shelter, and food preservation. Isolation is extreme.
examples: Fantasy: The Wall in A Song of Ice and Fire
entries.writing_tips: Cold is a character. It kills the careless, the unprepared, and the unlucky. Warmth and shelter become powerful dramatic tools. Isolation breeds both madness and self-reliance.

entries.title: Volcanic / Geothermal
entries.summary: Regions shaped by volcanic activity — fertile soil, geothermal energy, and constant geological threat.
entries.description: Volcanoes create rich soil for agriculture but threaten devastating eruptions. Hot springs, geysers, and lava tubes shape settlement patterns. Cultures may worship the volcano or develop early warning systems.
entries.writing_tips: Volcanoes are natural ticking clocks. The fertility-destruction duality creates communities that prosper in the shadow of doom. Eruptions make spectacular set pieces.

entries.title: Jungle / Rainforest
entries.summary: Dense, layered ecosystems teeming with life, danger, and hidden civilizations.
entries.description: Multiple canopy layers create distinct micro-environments. Extreme biodiversity provides medicines, poisons, and resources. Visibility is limited. Ruins hide under vegetation. Disease and predators are constant threats.
entries.writing_tips: The jungle swallows everything — paths, ruins, people. Characters fight the environment as much as enemies. Hidden temples and lost civilizations feel natural here.

entries.title: Barter Economy
entries.summary: Direct exchange of goods and services without currency.
entries.description: Trade happens through negotiation and equivalent exchange. Value is subjective and contextual. Reputation and personal relationships are essential for trade.
entries.writing_tips: Barter creates colorful market scenes. Characters with rare skills or goods have power. Lack of portable wealth changes travel and savings.

entries.title: Magical Economy
entries.summary: Economy where magic or magical resources serve as currency or primary commodity.
entries.description: Mana crystals, enchanted items, spell components, or magical services form the economic backbone. Magic users may be economic elite. Magical inflation and counterfeiting are possible crises.
entries.writing_tips: Consider what happens when magic is commodified. Who controls the supply? What can't be bought with magic?

entries.title: Feudal Economy
entries.summary: Land-based wealth system where agricultural output determines power.
entries.description: Wealth measured in land and the serfs who work it. Taxes paid in kind (grain, livestock). Limited currency circulation outside cities. Lords control trade through their territory.
entries.writing_tips: Land disputes drive feudal conflict. Harvest failures create famine and revolt. Characters' wealth is visible and territorial rather than abstract.

entries.title: Trade Networks / Silk Road
entries.summary: Long-distance trade routes connecting distant civilizations.
entries.description: Caravans, merchant ships, and trade posts link far-flung cultures. Exotic goods, ideas, diseases, and religions travel these routes. Control of trade nodes means enormous wealth and political influence.
entries.writing_tips: Trade routes are natural adventure paths. Merchants are information brokers. Bandits, tolls, and competing routes create conflict. Cultural exchange along trade routes drives worldbuilding.

entries.title: Guerrilla Warfare
entries.summary: Irregular combat using ambush, sabotage, and hit-and-run tactics by a smaller force.
entries.description: An outnumbered force uses terrain knowledge, civilian support, and mobility to resist a larger occupier. Blurs the line between civilian and combatant. Morale and popular support matter more than equipment.
entries.writing_tips: Guerrilla warfare puts characters in morally gray situations: collateral damage, informants, reprisals. The greatest weapon is patience and terrain knowledge.

entries.title: Siege Warfare
entries.summary: Extended military operation to capture a fortified position through encirclement and attrition.
entries.description: The attacker surrounds a fortification, cutting off supplies. The defender relies on provisions, fortifications, and hope of relief. Can last weeks to years. Includes mining, bombardment, starvation, and psychological warfare.
entries.writing_tips: Sieges are pressure cookers: dwindling supplies, disease, desperation. Both sides face hard choices. A siege compresses an entire war into one location.

entries.title: Naval / Maritime Warfare
entries.summary: Combat on seas and waterways using ships, marines, and naval strategy.
entries.description: Control of waterways determines trade and military reach. Ship types range from galleys to aircraft carriers. Weather, currents, and navigation are tactical factors. Boarding actions, cannon broadsides, and submarine warfare each create distinct combat.
examples: Fantasy: Ironborn in A Song of Ice and Fire
entries.writing_tips: Naval battles combine isolation (no retreat), technical skill (sailing), and the raw power of the sea. Ships are characters too — named, loved, and mourned.

entries.title: Magical Warfare
entries.summary: Conflict where magic is a primary weapon, defense, or strategic asset.
entries.description: Mages as artillery, magical shields, scrying for intelligence, teleportation for logistics. The rules of your magic system determine the tactics. Anti-magic countermeasures create an arms race.
entries.writing_tips: Ground your magical warfare in the rules you've established. The most interesting battles are won by clever use of limited magic, not by overwhelming power.

entries.title: Cold War / Proxy Conflict
entries.summary: Rival powers competing through espionage, diplomacy, and proxy wars rather than direct confrontation.
entries.description: Two or more major powers are too evenly matched or too afraid of mutual destruction to fight directly. Instead, they fund allies, conduct espionage, wage propaganda campaigns, and fight through proxies.
examples: Fantasy: political intrigue between great houses
entries.writing_tips: Cold wars are about paranoia, double agents, and the fear that one wrong move could trigger apocalypse. Spy characters live in moral ambiguity.

entries.title: Honor Culture
entries.summary: Society where personal and family honor governs behavior, reputation, and social standing.
entries.description: Insults must be answered. Promises are sacred. A person's word is their bond, and breaking it means social death. Duels, blood feuds, and elaborate codes of conduct maintain order. Shame is worse than death.
entries.writing_tips: Honor creates impossible dilemmas: when honor demands one thing and survival another. Characters trapped between conflicting honor obligations make compelling stories.

entries.title: Oral Tradition
entries.summary: Knowledge, history, and law preserved through spoken word, song, and performance.
entries.description: No writing system, or writing is reserved for elites. History is kept by bards, griots, or designated rememberers. Stories carry legal precedent, scientific knowledge, and cultural identity.
entries.writing_tips: Oral cultures value memory, performance, storytelling. Truth is fluid and shaped by the teller. Conflicting accounts drive intrigue. The 'last keeper of a story' is powerful.

entries.title: Rite of Passage
entries.summary: Ceremonial transition marking a change in social status, typically from youth to adulthood.
entries.description: A structured ordeal or ceremony that transforms a person's place in society. May involve physical trials, spiritual journeys, isolation, or demonstrations of skill. Failure can mean exile, delay, or death.
examples: Fantasy: Agiel in Wheel of Time
entries.writing_tips: Rites of passage are natural story structures: preparation, ordeal, transformation. Subvert by having characters fail, cheat, or discover the rite is corrupt.

entries.title: Taboo & Sacred
entries.summary: Things forbidden or revered by cultural consensus, often with supernatural justification.
entries.description: Taboos restrict behavior around food, death, sexuality, speech, or places. Sacred sites, objects, or practices are protected by tradition and fear. Breaking taboos may bring punishment from society or from the supernatural.
entries.writing_tips: Taboos create instant conflict when characters must break them. The tension between personal need and cultural prohibition drives character decisions.

entries.title: Hospitality Laws
entries.summary: Sacred obligation to protect and provide for guests, even enemies.
entries.description: Guests are inviolable under the host's roof. Breaking hospitality is one of the worst crimes. This creates safe havens in dangerous worlds, but also dramatic tension when enemies meet under hospitality protection.
examples: Fantasy: Guest right in A Song of Ice and Fire
entries.writing_tips: Hospitality laws create incredible dramatic tension. The Red Wedding works because it violates guest right. Characters may be trapped with enemies they cannot harm.

entries.title: Ancestor Worship
entries.summary: Veneration of deceased family members who may guide, protect, or curse the living.
entries.description: The dead remain part of the family. Rituals maintain connection. Ancestors may be consulted through oracles, dreams, or mediums. Neglecting ancestor rites brings misfortune. Family shrines are central to the home.
entries.writing_tips: Ancestor worship connects characters to their past and creates obligations to the dead. Family secrets literally haunt the living. Orphans without ancestors are culturally adrift.

entries.title: Stone Age / Neolithic
entries.summary: Pre-metal technology: stone tools, early agriculture, and the dawn of civilization.
entries.description: Flint knapping, fire management, early pottery, and the transition from hunter-gatherer to settled agriculture. Megaliths, cave art, and early religion. Communities are small and closely tied to the land.
entries.writing_tips: Stone age settings emphasize humanity's relationship with nature. Every tool is precious. Seasons and weather dominate life. Myths are alive and present.

entries.title: Bronze Age
entries.summary: Early metallurgy, city-states, writing systems, and organized religion emerge.
entries.description: Copper and tin alloys enable better tools and weapons. City-states develop with walls, granaries, and temples. Writing appears for record-keeping. Social stratification increases. Chariots dominate warfare.
entries.writing_tips: Bronze Age settings feel mythic and grand. Heroes are larger than life, gods walk among mortals, and the world feels new and dangerous.

entries.title: Iron Age / Classical
entries.summary: Iron weapons democratize warfare; empires, philosophy, and complex governance emerge.
entries.description: Iron is cheaper and more abundant than bronze, enabling larger armies. Roads, aqueducts, and engineered cities appear. Written law codes, philosophy, and organized military transform society.
entries.writing_tips: Classical settings offer sophisticated politics, military campaigns, and philosophical debate alongside brutal warfare and slavery. Grand in scale.

entries.title: Medieval / Dark Ages
entries.summary: Post-collapse rebuilding with feudal organization, castles, and the church as knowledge-keeper.
entries.description: Centralized authority has fragmented. Local lords provide protection in exchange for service. Castles dot the landscape. The church preserves literacy and learning. Plagues, crusades, and feudal warfare define the era.
entries.writing_tips: The most common fantasy technology level. Familiar enough for readers, limited enough that individual skill matters. Knights, castles, and swords.

entries.title: Renaissance / Early Modern
entries.summary: Gunpowder, printing, exploration, and the rebirth of classical knowledge.
entries.description: Gunpowder changes warfare. The printing press democratizes knowledge. Ocean exploration opens new worlds. Banking and mercantilism create new wealth. Artists, scientists, and explorers push boundaries.
entries.writing_tips: The Renaissance is about old certainties crumbling. Science vs. faith, old nobility vs. new merchants, known world vs. unknown lands. Rich for character conflict.

entries.title: Steampunk / Industrial
entries.summary: Victorian-era technology powered by steam, clockwork, and early electricity.
entries.description: Steam engines, railways, telegraphs, and factories transform society. Urbanization, class struggle, and colonialism accelerate. Technology is visible, mechanical, and audible.
entries.writing_tips: Steampunk contrasts technological marvel with social misery. Smog-choked cities, child labor, and mad inventors coexist.

entries.title: Magitech
entries.summary: Technology powered by or integrated with magic, blending the arcane and the mechanical.
entries.description: Magic and technology are complementary. Enchanted engines, spell-powered networks, magical computing, and arcane manufacturing. May replace, augment, or compete with conventional technology.
entries.writing_tips: Consider accessibility (who can afford enchanted goods?), dependency (what if magic fails?), and disruption (magical industrial revolution).

entries.title: Post-Apocalyptic
entries.summary: Civilization has collapsed; survivors scavenge, rebuild, and face new threats.
entries.description: After nuclear war, plague, magical cataclysm, or environmental collapse. Old technology becomes treasure. New societies form in the ruins. Knowledge is lost and rediscovered. The old world is both revered and feared.
entries.writing_tips: Post-apocalyptic settings are about what we keep and what we lose. The contrast between old-world artifacts and new-world reality creates poignant moments.

entries.title: Polytheism
entries.summary: Worship of multiple gods, each governing different domains of life.
entries.description: A pantheon of deities with distinct personalities, domains, and rivalries. Gods may be petty, benevolent, or indifferent. Mortals may play gods against each other. Temples, priests, and festivals dedicated to specific gods.
entries.writing_tips: Polytheistic worlds are colorful — gods can appear as characters, disagree with each other, and create competing demands on mortals. Divine politics mirror mortal politics.

entries.title: Monotheism
entries.summary: Belief in a single supreme deity who is the source of all creation and moral law.
entries.description: One God, often all-knowing and all-powerful. Organized church hierarchy interprets divine will. Heresy and schism are existential threats. The problem of evil (why does suffering exist if God is good?) is central.
examples: Fantasy: The Maker in Dragon Age
entries.writing_tips: Monotheistic settings create strong moral frameworks that characters can embrace, question, or rebel against. Religious institutions become political powers.

entries.title: Animism
entries.summary: Belief that spirits inhabit all things — rocks, rivers, trees, animals, and places.
entries.description: The world is alive with spirits. Every location, object, and creature has a spiritual dimension. Shamans mediate between the spirit world and the physical world. Rituals maintain balance. Offending a spirit brings consequences.
entries.writing_tips: Animistic worlds are inherently magical and alive. Characters must negotiate with the land itself. Environmental destruction has immediate spiritual consequences.

entries.title: Ancestor Veneration
entries.summary: The dead remain active participants in family and community life.
entries.description: Deceased ancestors watch over, guide, and can punish the living. Regular offerings, prayers, and rituals maintain the relationship. Genealogy is sacred. The unburied or forgotten dead become dangerous.
entries.writing_tips: Creates immediate personal stakes in religious practice. Characters carry their family's expectations beyond the grave. Orphans and outcasts lose this spiritual protection.

entries.title: Philosophy as Religion
entries.summary: Ethical and metaphysical systems that function as religion without traditional deities.
entries.description: Buddhism, Stoicism, Confucianism — organized systems of thought that provide moral guidance, community, and meaning without requiring belief in gods. May coexist with or replace traditional religion.
entries.writing_tips: Philosophical 'religions' emphasize internal discipline and right action. Characters face tests of principle rather than tests of faith. The struggle is with oneself.

entries.title: The Chosen One
entries.summary: A character destined by prophecy or fate to save the world or fulfill a grand purpose.
entries.description: Prophecy marks one individual as uniquely capable of defeating evil or restoring balance. The burden of destiny clashes with personal desire. The prophecy may be misinterpreted, self-fulfilling, or deliberately manipulated.
entries.writing_tips: Subvert by questioning the prophecy's source, having the chosen one fail or refuse, or revealing the prophecy was manufactured. The most interesting chosen ones resist their destiny.

entries.title: The Mentor
entries.summary: A wise guide who teaches the protagonist essential skills or knowledge before departing.
entries.description: The mentor provides what the protagonist lacks: training, wisdom, context, or confidence. The mentor often has a dark past or hidden agenda. Their departure (death, betrayal, or withdrawal) forces the protagonist to stand alone.
entries.writing_tips: The mentor's exit is as important as their presence. Consider giving mentors flaws, secrets, and their own arc. The best mentors are wrong about something important.

entries.title: The Trickster
entries.summary: A character who disrupts order through cunning, deception, and humor.
entries.description: Neither purely good nor evil, the trickster challenges authority, breaks rules, and creates chaos that sometimes helps and sometimes harms. They reveal hypocrisy and force change. Often the most entertaining character.
entries.writing_tips: Tricksters are catalysts — they don't change themselves but change everyone around them. Their unpredictability keeps readers guessing. Give them a hidden vulnerability.

entries.title: The Anti-Hero
entries.summary: A protagonist who lacks conventional heroic qualities but serves the narrative's moral center.
entries.description: Morally gray, selfish, ruthless, or broken — but ultimately on the side the reader roots for. Their methods are questionable but their goals may be just. They challenge the reader's moral assumptions.
entries.writing_tips: Anti-heroes need a line they won't cross, even if that line keeps moving. The reader must understand WHY they are the way they are. Redemption arcs are optional.
